news.title: Independent, Gen Z and Latino voters helped deliver a Democratic wave in 2026 – but that doesn’t mean a lasting realignment
news.text:
The Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections raises an important question about American politics. Are independent, Gen Z and Latino voters building a new Democratic coalition, or are they sending a warning to both parties that their support cannot be taken for granted?

The preliminary evidence suggests something more complicated.

Our analysis, including a deep dive into the 2026 Voter Poll conducted by the market research firm SSRS, points to three factors behind the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories: a substantial shift among independent voters toward Democratic candidates, stronger Democratic turnout relative to Republicans, and declining enthusiasm among voters who supported Donald Trump in 2024. 

Gen Z, who are people born from 1997 to 2012, and Latino voters played important roles in these shifts.

But the results should not automatically be interpreted as a lasting Democratic realignment. These voters may be demonstrating a willingness to reconsider their political choices when governing parties fail to meet their expectations.

The overlapping influence of independent, younger and Latino voters helps explain the scale of the Democratic gains. Our analysis, based on voter poll data, suggests that independents, who made up about one-third of voters, contributed approximately 52% of the Democrats’ national popular vote margin in House races. Latino voters contributed an estimated 23% of that margin, while voters ages 18 to 29 contributed approximately 39%. 

Because these groups overlap, their contributions cannot be added together. But the figures illustrate how important each was to the Democratic advantage.

In our book, “The Independent Voter,” co-authored with Omar Ali, we examine the growing influence of independent voters and their often unpredictable voting behavior.

Independents helped determine the outcome

Independent voters, among the most important contributors to Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms, have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to shift between parties.

In 2008, they favored Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama by 8 percentage points. Four years later, they backed Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney by 5 points. In the 2016 presidential election, independents favored Republican Trump by 4 points before swinging toward Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, supporting him by 13 points. 

In the 2024 presidential election, independents narrowly favored Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump, 49% to 46%. However, Trump performed better among independents in key battleground states, including Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and North Carolina.

In our research spanning nearly five decades, Dan Hunting and I, Thom Reilly, found that independents exhibit considerably greater volatility in their voting patterns than Democrats and Republicans.

The 3-point advantage independents gave Harris in 2024 provides a useful baseline for understanding their much larger shift toward Democratic candidates in 2026. A November 2026 national survey of more than 90,000 people found that voters identifying with neither major party favored Democratic House candidates by more than 20 percentage points.

Our analysis of voter poll data showed that independents favored House Democrats by 59% to 37%. In addition, independents’ support was consequential in several Republican-held Senate seats that flipped to Democrats, with independent voters providing the margin needed for victory in six of the nine races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Ohio and South Carolina. 

The emerging pattern may represent another turn in a longer cycle of electoral volatility among independents. Rather than embracing either party, independent voters appear willing to reconsider their choices as political and economic conditions change.

Did Republicans switch sides or stay home?

There is some disagreement about what produced the midterm Democratic wave.

Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston argue that Republican abstention – those who chose not to vote – was more important nationally than large-scale partisan crossover voting. They report that only approximately 6% of self-identified Republicans voted for Democratic House candidates.

Yet the evidence also demonstrates some crossover voting.

An analysis by the research firm NORC found that approximately 1 in 10 2024 Trump voters in 2026 supported Democratic Senate candidates in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina and Texas.

Both dynamics appear to have played a role. 

Democrats benefited from stronger participation among their supporters and reduced turnout among some voters who backed Trump in 2024. In several competitive races, Republican defections and strong independent support also contributed to Democratic victories.

Understanding these differences is important. A shift in election results does not necessarily mean voters have changed their party loyalties. It may reflect changes in who participates. The 2026 results suggest that both factors were at work.

Younger voters shifted sharply toward Democrats

Gen Z voters were another important part of the Democratic gains.

In 2026, 66% of voters ages 18–29 supported Democratic House candidates, compared with 30% who backed Republicans. That 36-point Democratic advantage was substantially larger than the 14-point margin in 2024, according to Tufts University.

There was also evidence of voters switching party choices. Among young people who voted for Trump in 2024 and participated in the 2026 election, 16% supported a Democratic House candidate. And 67% of young voters disapproved of Trump’s performance as president in 2026.

Gallup found that 56% of Gen Z adults identify as political independents, underscoring the weaker ties many younger Americans have to the two major parties. 

Combined with economic dissatisfaction and distrust of political institutions, this suggests that younger voters may be especially willing to reconsider their choices when the party in power fails to meet their expectations or deliver on its promises.

Latino voters also shifted substantially

Latino voters showed a similar pattern, but with some differences.

More than 6 in 10 Latino voters supported Democratic House candidates in 2026, according to a NORC survey. That reverses much of the Republican gains among these voters in 2024.

There was also evidence of volatility among Latinos. A postelection survey by UnidosUS and BSP Research found that 17% of Latino voters who supported Trump in 2024 voted for Democratic House candidates in 2026, compared with just 3% of Harris voters who supported Republicans.

Texas offers an example of how these voting groups overlapped.

According to our analysis of the voter poll data, 68% of Latino voters supported Democrat James Talarico, compared with 30% who backed his Republican opponent. Among voters ages 18 to 29, Talarico won 79% to 19%, while independents favored him by 64% to 33%.

Of course, these groups overlap. A voter can be Latino, young and independent, so their contributions cannot simply be added together numerically.

Still, Latinos’ strong support for Talarico illustrates how shifts among these voting groups helped Democrats win in a traditionally Republican state, perhaps shaping a new composite demographic.

A warning for both political parties

The lesson of 2026 may be less about Democratic realignment than about political accountability.

Republicans benefited in 2024 from dissatisfaction with Democratic governance. Two years later, Democrats benefited from dissatisfaction with Republican governance.

Yet the scale of the Democratic victories should not be understated. 

Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump’s presidency – his handling of the economy, the war in Iran, harsh immigration enforcement policies and concerns about corruption – contributed to a sweeping rejection of his administration and Republican leadership at both the federal and state levels. That includes a Congress that many voters believed had failed to hold him accountable.

Even so, neither party should assume that independents, younger voters or Latinos now belong to its camp.

America’s founders recognized the dangers of excessive party loyalty. In his 1796 farewell address, George Washington warned about the divisive influence of political parties and the dangers of placing party allegiance above the public interest.

More than two centuries later, the growing influence of voters with weaker ties to the major parties raises a similar question about the role of political parties in American democracy.

The 2026 election may not signal a lasting political realignment. Instead, it may reflect an electorate increasingly willing to hold both parties accountable.

For Democrats and Republicans alike, winning an election does not necessarily mean winning voters’ lasting loyalty.
news.summary: Midterm election results do not necessarily mean voters have changed their party loyalties. Instead, it may reflect an electorate increasingly willing to hold both parties accountable.

news.title: A Tiny Firm Was Hired to Run ICE’s Biggest Detention Facility. Here’s How It All Imploded.
news.text:
Back in January, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) announced two deaths at Camp East Montana, the nation’s biggest immigrant detention center. At the time, the facility at Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas, was operated by a tiny contractor most people had never heard of.

The agency reported that Geraldo Lunas Campos, a 55-year-old from Cuba, had been found “in distress” and died after “lifesaving measures.” Victor Manuel Diaz, a 36-year-old from Nicaragua, had been found with “a ligature around his neck”—likely suicide.

ICE, it turns out, didn’t share the full story. By the end of January, a medical examiner had determined that Lunas Campos actually died by homicide—guards asphyxiated him while restraining him to stop him from self-harm. Now, records obtained in a Freedom of Information Act request show that ICE privately blamed its contractor for failing to stop Diaz’s death—so much so, that the agency cited it as one of multiple reasons for ending the company’s roughly $1.3 billion contract.

The records are communications between ICE and the contractor, Acquisition Logistics, a small Virginia-based company that went from relative obscurity to the subject of national headlines after the Trump administration asked it to build and manage Camp East Montana in 2025. At the time, it had no prior experience in incarceration and was so small it operated out of a single-family home. Archived screenshots of its website—whose header simply said “Site maintenance in progress”—showed it had once specialized in supply chain management.

When ICE ended its contract in March, a year and a half early, the agency didn’t elaborate publicly on the reason, simply saying a bigger company would possess the “size, maturity and pedigree” to implement “higher standards of medical care, more thorough case processing and intake procedures, and delivery of performance requirements according to well-defined accountability measures.” The records Mother Jones obtained include “Contract Discrepancy Reports” and other documents that outline, in more detail, exactly what standards were not met—and the deadly consequences.

Acquisition Logistics’ relationship with ICE soured quickly, the records show. In the beginning, its main point of contact for Camp East Montana was not the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), but the Pentagon: Even though the camp would detain immigrants, the Navy had awarded the contract. “It’s weird,” Charles Tiefer, a professor emeritus of government contracting at the University of Baltimore law school, told me at the time.

“It seems messy,” added Claire Trickler-McNulty, who served as an ICE official in the Obama, Biden, and first Trump administrations.

As I reported then, DHS had tried to award the contract before the Navy did, to a firm called Deployed Resources, but canceled the deal days later “for convenience,” according to a government website that cited an executive order about “wasteful spending.” 

This was an extremely unusual move, and some current and former ICE officials speculated that -Deployed lost the job for political reasons. The Washington Free Beacon reported in 2023 that Deployed had snagged no-bid contracts for immigrant detention under President Joe Biden, and that a member of its board was married to the former chief of staff for Kamala Harris’ husband, Doug Emhoff. (The DC Enquirer called it “Kamala’s cronyism.”) A DHS spokesperson dismissed this as speculation, saying the contract was canceled due to an “inability to meet the specialized needs of the facility.”

Not long after ditching Deployed, ICE put the Fort Bliss contract out for bids again, and then quickly pulled it a second time, without explanation. The job went to Acquisition Logistics in the summer of 2025 under a Navy special contracting program in which only small businesses could apply. “If you want a detention center run by people who know what they’re doing, you hold serious competition, but that takes time,” Tiefer, the contracting expert, told me. “This is the third time they’re trying to make a procurement, and they’re under the gun—gotta get those detention centers up and running, gotta meet the quota. They were just betting [Acquisition Logistics] would have the minimum competence to hold the thing together, join in picking the subcontractors, and supervise them.”

It was “an absolute rush,” says Congresswoman Veronica Escobar, an El Paso Democrat whose district includes the camp. “Donald Trump and Stephen Miller wanted to do it the easiest, quickest way possible.”

Things went about as smoothly as one might expect. Although Camp East Montana was up and running in impressive time—ground broke in July 2025 and new detainees were arriving by August—a worker died during construction and, by September, journalists were documenting horrific conditions inside. ICE’s own inspectors found 60 violations of federal detention standards in 50 days, the Washington Post reported. “That was somewhat shocking,” recalls Michelle Brané, who led the Biden administration’s Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, the main oversight body for ICE detention. 

It’s not unusual for a new detention facility to have problems, so the best practice is to open it slowly—but that didn’t happen here, says former ICE official Trickler-McNulty, who has worked on contracts and detention standards. “None of it sounds like good governance,” she told me.

In October 2025, after Camp East Montana was operational, the administration transferred oversight of Acquisition Logistics’ contract from the Pentagon to ICE, according to emails I obtained. Later that month, an ICE contracting officer wrote CEO Ken Wagner to say that the funding wasn’t officially locked in yet, but that the company should proceed anyway because the work was “mission-essential.”

Wagner agreed, but by November 2025, emails show that his firm was desperate for cash. (Many federal contractors have struggled to be reimbursed promptly on Trump’s watch, according to Brané.) “As a small business, ALC and subs cannot continue to perform at such a high risk. Payrolls have to be met, vendors have to be paid, and it really is a crisis situation,” a company rep wrote to ICE.

Some funding came through soon after, but the relationship remained strained. On December 11, Wagner explained in a letter that ICE’s communications with his team had been “ineffective and, at times, perceived as threatening.”

“This has created an environment of uncertainty, hindered productive dialogue, and is creating significant concerns between ALC and our subcontractors,” he wrote. With discussions “eroding,” Wagner added, he was seeking “assistance in resetting our relationship to move forward in a more productive fashion.”

He provided excerpts from the allegedly threatening communications—all redacted in the documents I received. But other records show that ICE had expressed concerns over Acquisition Logistics’ lapse of liability insurance, a detainee’s escape, and problems with medical care. The agency had even sent a “Show Cause Notice” to the company in early October, days after taking control of the contract. “[Y]ou are hereby provided the opportunity to present any facts or explanations that demonstrate why the contract should not be terminated,” an ICE officer had written.

It had been complicated, Wagner said in his letter, for his company to transition from Pentagon to DHS control and navigate the agencies’ different expectations. He remained worried about a “lack of payment 75 days into the Option Period,” which posed “unnecessary and significant risks” to his business.

“Despite our repeated efforts to seek clarification and guidance, ALC has not received a government response to our concerns, leading to resource inefficiencies in our operations,” Wagner wrote. He requested a meeting with ICE officials to discuss solutions and figure out how to stop “de-railing productive hours” to messy back-and-forth.

Little seemed to improve. In February, an ICE contracting officer sent Acquisition Logistics another “Show Cause Notice” threatening to end the partnership. The CEO likely understood what this meant, Tiefer told me: “He can hear they’re clicking the rifle bolts on the firing squad. He’s writing his will at this point.”

The camp’s security protocols were not up to standard either, ICE said. In January, an officer’s firearm had gone missing, along with the spare key to the locker where it was stored. Transportation delays resulted “in significant operational disruptions” and janitorial services were inadequate. Housing units were supposed to be cleaned daily by staff, but an inspection found they were cleaned only once a week—and that guards had, on occasion, convinced detainees to clean for them by offering cookies.

Some of these allegations appeared in a Government Accountability Office report over the summer and received media coverage, but the records I obtained from ICE went into greater detail.

For one, in February, subcontractor Amentum Services “unilaterally” decided to cut detainees’ food intake below the contractual minimum of 3,000 calories a day. This deprivation resulted in “active hunger strikes” and “threats of riots,” ICE wrote. (Neither Amentum nor Acquisition Logistics and ICE responded to requests for comment for this story.)

Another subcontractor, Akima, let its guards track daily operations at the facility in a damaged logbook with missing pages—which became a problem, ICE wrote, after Geraldo Lunas Campos died. A witness told the Associated Press that Lunas Campos was handcuffed, tackled by guards, and put in a chokehold until he went unconscious. ICE’s report offered new details: Lunas Campos was restrained on the ground by four officers after he’d tried to hang himself, it said. One officer placed an arm around the man’s neck and another around his armpits with clasped hands, and all four officers were on top of him. When they eventually turned Lunas Campos on his side, he was unresponsive, with vomit on the floor.

“Lack of timely and complete information regarding the destruction of the logbook impeded the [Detainee Death Review] panel’s ability to establish an accurate timeline and conduct a thorough review,” ICE wrote, and also to assess officers’ compliance with use-of-force standards.

Lunas Campos’ family is suing Acquisition Logistics, Akima, and the guards for wrongful death, according to an attorney representing them, Will Horowitz, who told me it’s unclear whether the incident was adequately investigated by the government. “There’s so little that has been said in public about this.”

Another serious allegation involved the case of Victor Manuel Diaz, who was shipped to Camp East Montana after ICE arrested him on January 6 in Minnesota.

Eight days later, ICE wrote in its notice to Acquisition Logistics, custody officers moved Diaz from his dormitory to a medical holding room after he said he’d experienced harassment and “possible sexual abuse”—a detail that hadn’t been publicly reported, according to Rep. Escobar. (ICE has only cited the alleged harassment.) Diaz was scheduled for a Prison Rape Elimination Act interview. A behavioral health provider wrote that he had a “disheveled appearance, depressed mood, flat affect, and low, quiet speech,” though he’d denied that he was contemplating suicide.

ICE’s detention standards require placing at-risk detainees in suicide-resistant cells with “constant or close monitoring”—specifically, at irregular intervals no more than 15 minutes apart. But Diaz was put in a holding room with less frequent monitoring “despite risk indicators,” the agency wrote. He was observed awake at 2 p.m. and asleep at 2:30 p.m. and 3 p.m., the log indicated. Half an hour later staff found him hanging from a sheet he’d removed from his bed. 

Staffers took Diaz’s body down and placed it on the bed. Failing to find a pulse, camp medical personnel began CPR and other emergency measures. He was officially pronounced dead at 4:09. Although the “medical response was initiated promptly after discovery,” ICE noted, “the timeline indicates a possible delay in recognizing the emergency and notifying ICE”—and CPR should not have been performed on a soft surface like the bed. “The incident suggests a lack of staff vigilance and possible gaps in suicide prevention training, as staff failed to identify and respond to risk factors and did not maintain required observation protocols.”

ICE wrote that it had reviewed several cases of suicidal detainees at Camp East Montana in which officers hadn’t checked in at staggered 15-minute intervals as required—this problem has plagued ICE detention under past administrations as well, Brané told me. “Detainees on suicide watch are being placed in cells that contain objects and elements that can be used for self-harm,” ICE officials wrote, citing metal benches in holding cells, pony walls around toilets, and instruments affixed to the walls of medical bays.

Camp East Montana, the officials noted, also lacked policies to safely remove a person from suicide watch—one detainee, name redacted, was taken off watch despite suicidal ideation and a plan to act on it. And though detainees are supposed to receive mental health screening within 12 hours of admission, at least one wasn’t screened for about a month, despite indications of mental illness, the agency wrote. 

Months before Diaz’s death, ICE also had raised concerns with Acquisition Logistics because the facility’s medical holding rooms lacked “vision panel doors” that would allow officials to monitor the people inside; the company had promised to install the panels but hadn’t. The “failure to promptly address a previously identified and documented security deficiency,” its notice said, “represents a significant lapse in corrective action and facility safety management, and is a material contributing factor in the inability to prevent or timely intervene in the suicide of Mr. Diaz.”

“This incident resulted in the loss of life and exposes the facility, staff, and detainees to increased risk,” ICE added.

“This was a known screw-up,” Tiefer says of the vision panel doors. It seems “the suicide was the straw that broke the camel’s back and led ICE to dump Acquisition Logistics.”

Diaz had entered the United States in 2024 and was working to send money home to his family in Nicaragua, to help them save for a house. “Victor was law-abiding. He had never been in trouble in Nicaragua and, as we understand, was detained by ICE for missing an immigration court date—not for any crime,” his family said in a statement after his death.

In late February, 24 members of Congress wrote to DHS, citing safety concerns and calling for Camp East Montana to be “shut down.” On March 3, ICE sent another notice of “non-conforming performance” that again highlighted Diaz’s death and the infrequent cleaning of housing units, along with a detainee’s escape in October. Ten days later, it announced publicly that the contract would be terminated and that Amentum, the subcontractor that had cut meals to less than 3,000 calories, would take over. Amentum was a much bigger firm, with a long history of federal contracting. But conditions at the facility remained dire afterward, according to a lawsuit against ICE that cites, among other problems, medical neglect, staff violence, and inadequate food.

ICE apparently wasn’t “seeking a huge change if they just signed a contract with a vendor that was already running parts of the facility they were ostensibly unhappy with,” says Trickler-McNulty, the former ICE official, when I asked about the inadequate meals. But the administration “wants this facility; they likely didn’t want disruption in detention services, so they signed the agreement.”

Brané views the contract swap as a sign of just how bad conditions had become under Acquisition Logistics: worse than even ICE could tolerate. But “it’s probably gotten just as bad at a lot of facilities,” she says, noting that DHS shut down the independent oversight office she used to lead. “We are hearing more and more of these kinds of things, and there is no place to file a complaint and have it addressed, and so conditions have deteriorated across the board.”

Rep. Escobar told me she is glad Acquisition Logistics was fired and that she wants the company to be investigated. But she says it’s not the only entity that should be held accountable. For months, detainees had told her about poor conditions, but the career ICE personnel working at the facility brushed her off. They were “saying, ‘It’s all a lie,’ and it wasn’t,” she says. “They know better. There should have been alarm bells screaming up and down the chain.”

The administration should have forced Acquisition Logistics to address deficiencies immediately—or fired the company quicker, she says. Normally, Trickler-McNulty adds, ICE would use financial sanctions to hold a company accountable for problems early on, but the records we obtained show no signs of that. “There’s blame to be laid not just at the contractor’s feet,” Escobar says. “We have an obligation in Congress to look at the enablers.”

news.title: Latinos overwhelmingly voted for Gov. Katie Hobbs in midterm election
news.text:
Latino voters in Arizona overwhelmingly supported Gov. Katie Hobbs in the Nov. 3 midterm election, helping propel the Democratic incumbent to a decisive victory over Republican challenger Rep. Andy Biggs, according to a survey of Latino voters.

Seventy percent of Latino voters cast ballots for Hobbs compared to 24% for Biggs, according to the survey by UnidosUS, the Latino Community Foundation and BSP Research.

Hobbs defeated Biggs by more than 13 percentage points among all voters.

Hobbs received the highest percentage of support from Latino voters in any of the five gubernatorial races where Latino voters were surveyed, which included California, Michigan, Florida and Texas, according to the poll.

The resounding support for Hobbs from Latino voters in Arizona was in part a repudiation of President Donald Trump and his tough immigration crackdown and mass deportation policies, which have resulted in family separations that heavily impacted Latinos and put a target on Latinos who are United States citizens, said Arizona State University political scientist Stella Rouse, director of ASU's Hispanic Research Center.

Latino voters associated Biggs, a staunch ally of Trump who represented Arizona's 5th Congressional District for a decade, with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, Rouse said.

"To many Latinos, Biggs was an extension of the Trump administration and the harsh immigration policies that have come down the pike," Rouse said. "Biggs did nothing to separate himself from Trump on really any issue, but particularly on immigration and showed little indication that there would be a lot of daylight between him and Trump if he were to get elected."

Many Latino voters, especially younger voters, come from families that include a mixture of immigration statuses, including undocumented immigrants, or they know people who are undocumented, Rouse said.

Many Latino voters have felt personally targeted by ICE's aggressive immigration arrests even though they are U.S. citizens, Rouse said.

"They've arrested folks who are here legally in the country or have an asylum case pending and have even arrested U.S. citizens. So I think Latinos, even if they are here legally or even U. S. citizens, they don't feel safe from the deportation efforts that the Trump administration has engaged in."

Seventy-eight percent of Latinos in Arizona support creating a path to permanent legal status and citizenship for long-residing undocumented immigrants who pass a background check and pay a fine, according to the UnidosUS poll.

Ninety-three percent of Latino voters, including 89% of 2024 Trump voters, agreed with the statement: "We need a balanced and orderly integration system that has an earned citizenship for long-term residents, focuses enforcement inside the country on keeping communities safe with clear accountability, offers legal ways to immigrate that help our families and the economy, and keeps the border secure."

"This is a consensus position on immigration," said Gary Segura, president of BSP Research, a polling firm that conducted the survey.

The UnidosUS survey polled 10,000 voters, including 3,050 Latino voters, with 337 in Arizona.

Oversamples were conducted in Arizona, California, Florida, Texas and Michigan in the U.S. House and Senate battlegrounds. The survey had an overall margin of error of 1.8%, and 5.3% in Arizona.

Other key Arizona highlights from the survey:

Democratic House members received more support from Latino voters than in any of the five states where Latinos were surveyed. Democratic House candidates in Arizona received 73% of the Latino vote compared to 25% for Republicans, a difference of 48 percentage points.

Arizona is the only state where support for Democrats from Latino men was higher than that of Latina women. Latino men backed Democratic candidates for Congress 74% to 24%, a 50-point margin, compared with 71% to 27% among Latinas, a 44-point margin.

More: Latino 'anger,' 'peer pressure' helped Democrats win, group says

The GOP lost ground in Arizona in the November midterm compared to the 2024 election, when Trump won 43% of the Latino vote. Twenty percent of Latinos in Arizona who voted for Trump in 2024 backed Hobbs, and 16% backed Democratic House candidates. Only 2% of Latinos in Arizona who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 backed Biggs, and 1% backed Republican House candidates.

It is "absolutely not true" that Democrats have cemented the Latino vote despite the strong support Democrats received from Latino voters this year, Rouse said.

"The Latino vote is up for grabs," Rouse said. "Latinos are much less likely to be loyal to either political party and are much more likely to vote for issues than particular candidates."

Republicans have an opportunity to win back support from Latino voters in 2028 by focusing on issues Latinos care about, including affordability, jobs, health care, and education, Rouse said.

The November midterms also showed that Republicans need to dial back immigration arrests of undocumented workers who haven't committed crimes and focus on passing comprehensive immigration reforms that include pathways to legalization for some undocumented immigrants to win back support from Latino voters in 2028, Rouse said.

Sixty-one percent of Latino voters in Arizona cited the cost of living and inflation as one of the top three issues elected officials should address.

Thirty-nine percent cited jobs and the economy; 34% cited health care costs; and 24% cited affordable housing and rent. Groceries (57%); housing (41%); health care and prescription drugs (34%); utilities (33%); and gasoline (32%) led their cost-of-living concerns.

news.title: Trump Voters Give Brutal Verdict on Future of MAGA
news.text:
Republicans are rattled following the 2026 midterm elections bloodbath, and a growing number of them are losing faith.

One in five people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 are confident that the next occupant of the White House will be a Democrat.

That is according to a new poll, which shows a broad sense of apathy amongst the party after a lackluster first half of Trump’s second term.

Politico polled 2,000 adults in the week after the midterm elections, finding almost twice as many voters believe a Democrat was bound to win in 2028 as those who don’t. 

Only 60 percent of Republicans were still convinced the White House would remain red. 

But Democrats who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 were exceedingly confident, with 87 percent convinced their party would regain the presidency. 

What nobody seems sure about is who will secure either party’s nominations. With no clear frontrunner from either the Democrats or Republicans, debates and infighting are heating up behind closed doors.

Harris voters are split between wanting a “fighter” (43 percent), a “progressive” (40 percent), or a “creative” (30 percent). 

A surprising takeaway from the poll was that Trump voters are less enthusiastic about competitive politics going forward. 

Only 39 percent want another “fighter,” with 45 percent preferring a “conservative.”

Another point of contention is whether or not their next candidate should come from within Trump’s own inner circle. 

Nearly three in 10 Trump voters said they would rather see someone outside the current administration emerge to win the next election. That support balloons to 46 percent among Trump voters who don’t identify as MAGA. In contrast, 82 percent of MAGA diehards would prefer someone inside Trump’s circle as the next president.

The GOP’s disastrous midterm election results–losing control of both the House and the Senate– completely upended the party’s expectations of what would come next.

Vice President J.D. Vance had long been considered the frontrunner to replace the 80-year-old president, but that future is no longer so clear. And Trump himself has remained coy about who he will endorse. 

Vance is strongly tied to Trump and his near record-low approval ratings, the disastrous war in Iran, and voters massively rejecting the Republican Party and the MAGA movement as a whole.

But Vance has also split with Trump in blaming the midterm results on the war with Iran.

Trump’s own son is facing the same prospects, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey that asked Republican and Republican-leaning voters to rate a series of possible 2028 presidential contenders.

Donald Trump Jr. would make a “poor” candidate, according to 43 percent of those surveyed. 

Just 12 percent considered him “excellent,” while 17 percent said he would make a “good” candidate.

Republicans on the Hill are growing increasingly vocal in support of Secretary of State Marco Rubio to throw his hat in the ring, but even that is not guaranteed. 

Rubio has publicly ruled out a run for president if Vance announces a tilt in 2028, and insiders have also said the secretary would like an opportunity to step back from politics so that he can make some money in the private sector.

Chair of Michigan’s Shiawassee County Republican Party Dan McMaster said the party needs a candidate who is “as far away from Trump as possible.”

“And even then, I think it’s going to be a battle,” he told Politico.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Daily Beast.

One in five people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 are confident that the next occupant of the White House will be a Democrat.

That is according to a new poll, which shows a broad sense of apathy amongst the party after a lackluster first half of Trump’s second term.

news.title: Trump grows frustrated with Vance over Iran war critique, Times reports
news.text:
President Donald Trump has grown frustrated with Vice President JD Vance for blaming the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm losses, The New York Times reported Wednesday.

Trump has told aides and allies that Vance should have said the president was right to go to war with Iran, people familiar with his comments told the newspaper. In private, Trump has praised Secretary of State Marco Rubio and suggested he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to people who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Many Republicans have assumed Vance would lead the field for the 2028 Republican nomination, the Times reported, though Trump has wavered about him in public and private. Trump’s advisers say he is in no hurry to endorse a successor.

Vance wrote on social media the day after the midterms, “The reason we lost is the war.” His lengthy post criticized much of the administration’s pre-election messaging after Democrats won the largest midterm victory for either party since the post-Watergate elections. He also cited the U.S. relationship with Israel.

In the post, Vance said Trump had likewise attributed the losses to the war, although Trump has cited several factors, chiefly his own absence from the ticket. Vance had said when he endorsed Trump in 2023 that Trump would not drag the United States into new wars.

Trump initially told reporters, “I think it's largely true.”

Earlier this month, however, Trump said Vance should have “made one other statement.” “If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes,” Trump said of the point he believed was missing from the analysis.

Vance removed from Iran talks

Following Vance’s post, Trump announced that he was removing the vice president from Iran peace talks, which Vance had intensified shortly before the elections. Trump said he wanted Vance to concentrate instead on investigating allegations of fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

On Monday, Fox News asked Vance whether there was any “daylight” between him and Trump. “I think there's no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration,” Vance said.

Vance has told Fox News he has not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028. “We'll figure it out sometime next year,” he said.

His allies say he is genuinely undecided and cite his young family, including his fourth child, born in July. Some allies said a Trump decision to resume major combat operations in Iran would drastically reduce the chances of a Vance run.

Vance canceled a planned Wednesday appearance at the Times’ DealBook Summit, citing Washington meetings to address recent tech outages. The White House did not respond to the newspaper’s request for comment.

Alyssa Farah Griffin, a former White House aide in Trump’s first term and co-host of “The View,” told the Times that Vance’s “daylight” remark “may have seemed insignificant in the moment, but it will live in campaign ads.”

Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist and former deputy campaign manager to Kamala Harris, told the Times, “But you do have to feel for him because he's stuck. When you're the vice president, you're stuck.”

Trump praises Rubio

Rubio has had a prominent role during Trump’s trip abroad, while Vance has stayed in the United States. At the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila on Tuesday, Trump asked, “How hot is Marco, right?” and said Rubio has been “fantastic.”

Rubio told The New York Times earlier that Trump “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for authorizing strikes against Iran.

A Reuters poll cited by The Jerusalem Post found that 45% of Republican voters viewed Rubio as an “excellent” presidential candidate, compared with 43% for Vance. Completed Monday, the poll had a margin of error of five percentage points for Republican and Democratic voters.

Rubio has said he would support Vance and dismissed reports that he would leave the administration to run for president. Some Rubio allies, however, said he would run if Trump encouraged him.
news.summary: Vance blamed the war for Republican midterm losses; Trump later removed him from Iran peace talks.

news.title: Nearly twice as many Americans think the next president will be a Democrat: poll
news.text:
Nearly twice as many Americans think the next president will be a Democrat after the blue tsunami swept through red states in the midterms. 

Fifty-two percent of Americans think the nominee that the Democratic Party chooses in the 2028 election will take the White House, according to a new Politico poll. Just 28 percent said the Republican Party will take the win.

Just two years ago, Democrats were licking their wounds after Donald Trump beat then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Harris was chosen as the nominee after then-President Joe Biden dropped his reelection bid following a disastrous debate performance against Trump. 

But things are turning around big time for Democrats after they won control of the House and Senate, as well as historic gubernatorial races, earlier this month. While Trump has refused to take the blame for the GOP shellacking, he is facing record-low approval ratings with an unpopular war in Iran, stubborn inflation and an immigration agenda that many find too aggressive. 

Of those in the Political poll who voted for Harris in 2024, 87 percent say the Democrats will win the 2028 presidential election. Meanwhile, 60 percent of Trump 2024 voters say the Republican nominee will take the White House. 

“Whoever’s running for president has seen what’s happened and also has seen the power of our movement, and so this is something that could be carried on to 2028,” Representative-elect Adam Hamawy, a progressive New Jersey Democrat, told Politico.

Now the question is: who will run for president in 2028?

There are several names on both sides that have been floating since before the midterms. 

Forty-five percent of Democrats or Democratic-leaning respondents said Harris would be an excellent or good candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination in the 2028 election, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.

Biden’s former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg trailed, with 42 percent seeing him as an excellent or good candidate. California Governor Gavin Newsom followed, with 40 percent viewing him as an excellent or good candidate. 

Thirty-eight percent of Americans thought Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive from New York, and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, who recently won re-election after making headline-grabbing jabs at Trump, would be excellent or good candidates. 

Vice President JD Vance led other potential opponents in the poll, with 62 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning respondents believing he would be an excellent or good candidate for the GOP presidential nomination in the 2028 election. 

Another 58 percent said Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be an excellent or good choice, and 52 percent said the same for outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who unsuccessfully ran against Trump for the nomination in 2024. Thirty-five percent of Americans said Texas Senator Ted Cruz would make an excellent or good candidate.
news.summary: Names that have been floated as possible Democratic nominees include Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

news.title: NYTimes: Suuuure Looks Like Trump Is Leaning Away From Vance 2028
news.text:
Has Donald Trump decided to pass over J.D. Vance for the next generation of Republican/MAGA leadership? Or are the New York Times' sources spinning their own interests?

The answer could be both. The rumors do tend to fit the circumstances of the political moment. Trump has now pulled his VP off of two different tasks, and it's not too hard to believe that the boss is not pleased with Vance's attempt to blame Trump's war for the massive midterm losses:

The vice president, who endorsed Mr. Trump in 2023 saying he would not drag the United States into new wars, expressed reservations about the conflict privately inside the administration. But after the huge G.O.P. losses in this month’s midterms, he went public, laying out in blunt terms what he said went wrong.“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in his lengthy social media post the day after the midterms.Mr. Vance made the point of adding that Mr. Trump had also said as much — though the president has blamed Republicans’ losses on many factors, chiefly that he was not on the ticket.For Mr. Vance, it appeared to be an attempt to separate himself from the administration’s policy without criticizing the president. But Mr. Trump soon announced that he was pulling his vice president from engaging in peace talks with Iran, an effort that Mr. Vance had intensified shortly before the elections. Mr. Trump said he wanted Mr. Vance to focus on investigating allegations of fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

Vance's new withdrawal from a high-profile appearance today involves the NY Times. He was supposed to speak at their DealBook summit today but backed out, ostensibly to deal with Bugmageddon. Why that would require the VP to attend meetings is unclear, especially with every other Cabinet official telling the public that the outages are not connected to cyber warfare or hostile entities. Vance has suddenly gone from a valued administration surrogate to a cloistered existence, at least for the moment, following his public analysis of the midterms. 

The issue may not be the way Vance linked the midterms to the war, though. The NYT's Tyler Pager misses what may have angered Trump even more than the implicit criticism of Trump's decision to deal with Iran – J.D. Vance's declaration that we must "change our relationship to Israel." To what, exactly? Why would we want to change our relationship with the only liberal democracy in that region and a partner on intelligence in the most dangerous neighborhood in the world? Moreover, Trump's affinity for Israel is well known and has been one of the most consistent characteristics of his foreign policy. Any suggestion that the US distance itself from Israel would have likely offended Trump more than the obvious point about Americans tiring of gas prices and inflation resulting from the conflict with Iran. 

Oddly enough, Pager never mentions that part of Vance's criticism in his analysis. He only mentions Israel in relation to Kamala Harris' difficulties in separating herself from Joe Biden's tepid support of Israel. 

At any rate, Pager believes that the last two weeks have signaled that Trump has chosen Marco Rubio as his most likely successor:

But over the past two weeks, Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how his vice president framed his assessment of what went wrong, complaining to aides and allies that Mr. Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran, according to people with knowledge of the president’s comments.At the same time, Mr. Trump has continued to praise Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, in private conversations and suggesting that he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe discussions going on behind closed doors. Mr. Trump’s allies have noted that Mr. Rubio has repeatedly said the president’s move to attack Iran was essential for the country’s national security. ...The tension comes at a critical juncture for Mr. Vance, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028, a campaign in which Mr. Trump’s support could be critical to his ability to secure the Republican nomination. The president’s favorable comments about Mr. Rubio are the latest example of how Mr. Trump has been weighing the strengths of the two men as the question of his successor grows more urgent.

Er ... maaaaaybe. Trump has made his irritation with Vance known well enough, although without the usual public broadsides Trump routinely launches against his other critics. He certainly didn't appreciate having to deal with reporters asking him to respond to Vance's criticism. However, Trump's moods are mercurial, while his grasp of his own interests is not. He's married to Vance in the political sense, having chosen Vance as his partner in this term after sharply rebuffing his previous VP, Mike Pence. Trump will spend the next two years as most presidents do with their last years in office: staking "legacy" claims. A public break with Vance would not serve Trump's interests well, especially now that the GOP has to circle the wagons during that period of time.

In the end, the best bet would be that Trump won't pick a successor at all. If Vance or Rubio win the nomination, Trump can claim – legitimately – that his legacy will guide the party's future. If someone else from outside his administration wins it, such as Ron DeSantis, that claim will be harder to sustain, but Trump will have other accomplishments to tout nonetheless. Especially given the midterm results, Trump may well leave the succession question alone lest it backfire on Vance or Rubio. 

In other words, this is but a tempest in a teapot for all involved. Vance has to decide whether he wants to run at all, and in this environment ... it won't be an easy choice.

news.text:
WASHINGTON — At first, President Donald Trump appeared notably unfazed by Vice President JD Vance’s postelection analysis blaming the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.

“I think it’s largely true,” the president told reporters after Vance posted a lengthy missive on social media in which he also critiqued much of the administration’s messaging in the run-up to the elections.

But over the past two weeks, Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how his vice president framed his assessment of what went wrong, complaining to aides and allies that Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran, according to people with knowledge of the president’s comments.

At the same time, Trump has continued to praise Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, in private conversations and suggesting that he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe discussions going on behind closed doors. Trump’s allies have noted that Rubio has repeatedly said the president’s move to attack Iran was essential for the country’s national security.

Trump has hinted at his irritation with Vance in public, saying this month that the vice president should have “made one other statement.”

“If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes,” he said, laying out what he believes was missing from Vance’s analysis.

The tension comes at a critical juncture for Vance, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028, a campaign in which Trump’s support could be crucial to his ability to secure the Republican nomination. The president’s favorable comments about Rubio are the latest example of how Trump has been weighing the strengths of the two men as the question of his successor grows more urgent.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Vance’s office declined to comment, pointing to recent interviews the vice president has given.

When asked on Fox News this week about his postelection commentary and whether there was any “daylight” between him and the president, Vance said, “I think there’s no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration.”

On Wednesday, Vance canceled a planned appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit, citing meetings in Washington to address the recent tech outages.

Since Trump brought him aboard as his running mate for a second term, many Republicans have assumed that Vance, a former senator from Ohio, would be the front-runner for their party’s nomination in 2028. But Trump has waffled publicly and privately on his vice president throughout his tenure, and Vance says he has not decided whether to run for president.

“I haven’t made a decision,” he said on Fox News. “We’ll figure it out sometime next year.”

Allies of Vance, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, say he is genuinely undecided about his political future. They point to his young family (his fourth child was born in July) as one reason he might not mount a White House bid in 2028. They also note his obsession with political analysis and data and suggest that if he does not see a path to victory, he may sit out this race.

The fallout from the war with Iran — and its unpopularity among voters — could be a significant factor, too. Some allies of Vance say that if the president decides to resume major combat operations in Iran, it would drastically reduce Vance’s chances of running.

The vice president, who endorsed Trump in 2023 saying he would not drag the United States into new wars, expressed reservations about the conflict privately inside the administration. But after the huge GOP losses in this month’s midterms, he went public, laying out in blunt terms what he said went wrong.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in his lengthy social media post the day after the midterms.

Vance made the point of adding that Trump had also said as much — though the president has blamed Republicans’ losses on many factors, chiefly that he was not on the ticket.

For Vance, it appeared to be an attempt to separate himself from the administration’s policy without criticizing the president. But Trump soon announced that he was pulling his vice president from engaging in peace talks with Iran, an effort that Vance had intensified shortly before the elections. Trump said he wanted Vance to focus on investigating allegations of fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

Alyssa Farah Griffin, who worked in Trump’s White House during the first term and is now a co-host of “The View,” said a comment from Vance reminded her of a comment that Kamala Harris, then the vice president, made on the ABC show during the 2024 campaign. When asked if she would have done anything differently from President Joe Biden, Harris said, “There is not a thing that comes to mind.”

“JD Vance is in the impossible position that any Trump VP inevitably ends up in,” Griffin said. “He can’t have any separation or daylight from the president.”

Vance’s “daylight” comment this week “may have seemed insignificant in the moment, but it will live in campaign ads,” she added.

Vance’s allies say a competitive primary, not a coronation, will benefit the next Republican presidential nominee, and they cite Harris’ loss in 2024 as evidence of that theory. Harris quickly secured the Democratic nomination after Biden dropped out of the race, despite some Democrats’ calls for a more formal nominating process.

But Vance ultimately could find himself in a similar situation to Harris, who many voters saw as an extension of Biden, political strategists said. Even as she privately signaled she had concerns about Biden’s handling of the Israel-Hamas war, she was unable to figure out how to separate herself from the unpopular president.

“It’s very hard to get me to say that I have any amount of sympathy for JD Vance because he put himself in this position,” said Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist and former deputy campaign manager to Harris. “But you do have to feel for him because he’s stuck. When you’re the vice president, you’re stuck. In the Harris situation, there was not much you can actually do to separate yourself.”

Vance now must wrestle with that complex dynamic as he assesses the future of the Republican Party and in which direction he would try to lead it. His path to the vice presidency — from a “never Trumper” to Trump’s vice president — suggests that he could go in different directions.

Vance was an avowed critic of Trump in 2016, calling him “unfit for our nation’s highest office.” He then became a supporter of Trump and sought the president’s endorsement when he ran for a Senate seat in Ohio in 2022. He received the endorsement and won that race.

Many Republicans believe Vance would need the explicit, or at least implicit, support from Trump to win a Republican primary. But that is far from a guarantee. The president has always relished competition among his aides, and his advisers say he is in no rush to endorse a successor.

And after Republicans’ disastrous results in the elections this month, in which Democrats won the largest midterm victory for either party since the post-Watergate elections, other Republicans see an opening, too. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas and Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida are among those considering possible bids.

Then there’s Rubio. He has said he would support Vance and dismissed reports that he is going to leave the administration to run for president. But some of his allies said he would run if Trump encouraged him to do so — and Trump has not been shy about lavishing praise on him.

“How hot is Marco, right?” Trump said Tuesday at the ASEAN summit in Manila. “Is Marco doing a great job? He’s been fantastic.”

While Vance has remained in the United States, as the vice president does when the president travels abroad, Rubio is playing a prominent role on the president’s trip. On Tuesday, he addressed public fears about the multiple technology outages in the United States, seeking to reassure Americans that there was no evidence of cyberattacks.

Rubio’s defense of the Iran war, in particular, has earned him goodwill with the president.

In a recent interview with the Times, Rubio said Trump “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for authorizing strikes against Iran.

“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.

The distinct approaches of Rubio and Vance underscore a broader debate in the party — should the next Republican presidential candidate align themselves with Trump’s legacy?

Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey, who is considering another run for the White House, said Vance’s challenges transcend his unique position as vice president.

“I don’t think anyone that was part of Trump 2.0 will be able to win in the fall of 2028,” he said. “They will be billed as another four years of Donald Trump, and that will not be salable to the American people.”

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

The tension comes at a critical juncture for the vice president, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028.
