news.title: Republican Governor-Elect Nominates Lifelong Democrat To Be His Attorney General
news.text:
Republican Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow nominated a lifelong Democrat to be his state attorney general. 

Barlow nominated attorney Walter Eggers to be the next attorney general, who donated over $20,000 to Democrats in recent decades, Federal Elections Commission (FEC) filings show. Liberal donors, advocacy groups and corporate interests collectively played a key role in helping Barlow secure the Republican nomination and in ousting conservatives with liberal Republicans. 

Eggers confirmed to The Cowboy State Daily that he has been a lifelong Democrat. He argued that the difference between Democrats and Republicans in Wyoming is not as great as people suggest. 

Eggers donated $1,000 to former President Joe Biden’s campaign on Feb. 29, 2020, and $2,300 to former President Barack Obama’s campaign in 2008, FEC filings show. He donated over $18,000 to the Wyoming Democratic Party between 2004 and 2020. (RELATED: Grassroots Wyoming Conservatives Coalescing Around New Governor Candidate To Defeat Left-Leaning GOP Nominee)

Per FEC records, Eggers has given: $18,735 to the Wyoming Democratic Party (2004-2020) $2,300 to Barack Obama $1,800 to the DNC $1,250 to Hillary Clinton $1,000 to Joe Biden $250 to Kamala Harris (2024) For years, the state party got a check almost every month.— State Freedom Caucus Network (@SFC_Network) November 16, 2026

Barlow did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment. 

Barlow defeated Megan Degenfelder, who President Donald Trump endorsed, during the Aug. 18 primary. The Wyoming Freedom Caucus lost its majority in the state House after 13 incumbent members were defeated and four additional Freedom Caucus-aligned members lost their state Senate bids. 

The governor-elect defeated Democratic Wyoming gubernatorial candidate Ken Casner and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel with 68.1% of the vote. Bextel, who launched her campaign after the primary, came in second with 16.6% of the vote. Bextel told the DCNF that she launched her campaign to stop the left-leaning Barlow from becoming governor. 

“People understand how desperate it is,” Bextel told the DCNF in September. “So yes, I need all the help I can get, but I am fully expecting to win this race. And look, this should bring hope to everybody in Wyoming. If the establishment Republicans and establishment Democrats want the same thing, it takes the rest of us to fight for the American people.”

Barlow voted with a majority of Democrats 90% of the time and was the sixth most liberal Republican in the state House, according to Evidence Based Wyoming’s Doug Gerard. He was affiliated with the anti-coal, anti-oil and anti-gas Powder River Basin Resource Council. 

The governor-elect voted to raise taxes on the oil and gas industry, sponsored an amendment in 2014 to accept Obamacare funding in Wyoming and voted to change the definition of marriage, according to Gerard’s report.

Barlow received more than $1,000 from Rene Hinkle, a plaintiff in lawsuits challenging Wyoming’s abortion ban, according to Cowboy State Daily. A Barlow campaign spokeswoman said the donation and others reflected “what [Barlow] stands for. Which is respectful leadership. And he has a record on that.”

The Wyoming Donor Alliance, a non-partisan organization, outlined a plan to oust Freedom Caucus and Trump-endorsed candidates to replace them with less conservative Republicans. It created a strategy titled, “Break the Wyoming Freedom Caucus Majority,” according to documentation previously obtained by the DCNF. 

The plan intended to raise $839,500 to recruit candidates, target specific voters and endorse or oppose Freedom Caucus candidates. 

Wayne Hughes Jr., the owner of Cowboy State Daily, gave $15,000 to the Civil Leadership PAC, which spent about $200,000 backing non-Freedom Caucus Republicans in the primary, according to Transparency USA. The Civil Leadership PAC backed Short and Barlow, which Neiman and other conservatives argued were not true conservatives. 

The PAC spent $168,000 in expenditures to support Barlow’s gubernatorial bid, $19,000 to support Short and over $4,000 on Republican Wyoming state Rep. Steve Harshman, who won his primary in hopes of becoming the next superintendent of public instruction. Harshman defeated Republican Wyoming state Rep. Tom Kelly, who was backed by the Freedom Caucus, according to Cowboy State Daily.

A newly formed PAC called Common Sense Republicans for Wyoming endorsed Barlow and candidates running against Freedom Caucus members.
news.summary: Egger has donated thousands of dollars to Democrats
news.author: Nicole Silverio

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed 2028 Chances as Dem Strategist Sees Him as AOC Alternative
news.text: Democratic strategist Dan Turrentine said there is "almost a consensus" within his party that Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed would run for president in 2028 if Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who is seen as the favorite among many progressives, opts against standing. He said he saw the near consensus during the What’s Next conference, Democrats’ post-election conference in Denver, Colorado, over the weekend. He made the comments during a new episode of The Huddle podcast. "Because we have no front-runner, because we don’t even know if AOC is going to run, there’s increasing talk—one of the things when I left Saturday morning, there was almost a consensus that if AOC doesn’t run, El-Sayed is," he said. But El-Sayed has said he is "not running" and wants to focus on his job in the Senate. Turrentine's comments come just weeks after El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race by about 7 points, a major victory for the progressive left in one of the nation’s most closely divided swing states. With the midterms in the rearview, 2028 speculation has already begun in Washington. Democrats are preparing to launch presidential runs over the coming months as the party grapples with the direction it should take following their significant wins over Republicans earlier this month. Ocasio-Cortez, of New York, is frequently named as a potential presidential candidate who could consolidate support on the Democratic Party’s left due to her status as a well-known national figure who is popular among Democrats. But she has also been floated as a potential primary challenger to New York Senator Chuck Schumer, a Democrat who has caught the ire of the party’s progressive base. If Ocasio-Cortez chooses not to run for president, she may leave a gap in the primary, as it’s less clear who would be able to run in that progressive lane, which was occupied by Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders in 2016 and 2020. El-Sayed is among the left-leaning politicians who have been named as potential candidates. Abdul El-Sayed Downplayed 2028 Speculation El-Sayed, for his part, has downplayed speculation that he could run for 2028. He told progressive news outlet Zeteo after his victory he is "not running" for president and that his job is to be the "best senator" he can be. The incoming senator would face a difficult path to victory if he chooses to run due to what would be a very short stint in the Senate prior to his campaign, Todd Belt, director of the Political Management Program at The George Washington University, told Newsweek on Tuesday. "Democrats in the primaries will be looking for somebody who has some experience at delivering, and it's highly unlikely that El-Sayed will be able to have any sort of record of delivering within just a couple of years, maybe not even that, of being in the Senate without a filibuster-proof majority and a president who is guaranteed to veto quite a bit of the legislation that he would like to pass," he said. Democratic strategist Eddie Vale told Newsweek he is more skeptical about El-Sayed running. "He was just elected to Senate of course but I also think there is a much better case that he can build power and advocate for what he wants by being a key voice in the primary and general election in Michigan, and having other candidates seek out his support rather than throwing his hat in the ring and instantly becoming a target for everyone," he said. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed’s team for comment via email. Abdul El-Sayed’s Chances in 2028 Post-midterms polling on El-Sayed’s chances in 2028 has been limited, but one survey from The New York Times and Siena University published prior to the elections signaled that he would have a tough time in the primary field. Prediction markets are also not bullish on his chances. El-Sayed’s chances stood at less than half a percentage point in the Times poll, which surveyed 1,170 registered voters from October 12 to 19. Instead, it gave an edge to former Vice President Kamala Harris, who had support from 12 percent of respondents, followed by California Governor Gavin Newsom at 9 percent, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 7 percent and Ocasio-Cortez at 6 percent. Most voters—45 percent—were undecided. El-Sayed’s chances were also low on prediction markets—having just a 0.7 percent chance on Kalshi and a 1 percent chance on Polymarket as of Tuesday morning. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Is Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Running for President? Prominent progressives weighing presidential runs could be waiting to see what Ocasio-Cortez ultimately decides to do in 2028. She could run for president, challenge Schumer or even run for reelection to her House seat in New York’s 14th Congressional District. She has filed paperwork with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) to run for a sixth term in the House, but has not said for sure what her next steps will be. The filing on its own does not necessarily mean she will run for reelection—it only signals that she is keeping her options open. In September, she told the Times she expected to decide on a presidential run after the midterms. "I’m not naive to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latin," Ocasio-Cortez said. "And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities." Ocasio-Cortez previously addressed presidential speculation last May in a conversation with David Axelrod, a former adviser to former President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country," she said. "Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways…to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were seven years old, it is tremendously liberating." The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) passed a resolution titled "Run AOC 2028 To Win A Democratic Socialist President" during its November 14 convention, reported City & State New York. Could the Left Win in 2028? Debate over the direction of the party has already begun ahead of the next presidential election. Questions over whether progressives can actually win a national presidential contest have always been a point of contention for the left. Many Democrats believe someone who is more moderate will be better suited to win over independent voters and centrist Republicans. Progressives, however, believe someone on the left could convince disaffected Democrats to head to the polls. They argue midterm results, such as El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan or Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson’s victory over Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine, suggest that progressives can indeed win tough races. Belt said that progressives are in a better strategic position in terms of how they have conducted their campaigns ahead of 2028, even if that is not necessarily true in terms of policy. "The one thing I will say about the progressives is they are giving people something to vote for and not just against. That's something that the moderates and the establishment have really focused on, is stopping Trump. Okay, but how are you going to put money back in people's pockets?" he said. Still, he noted that the map is going to be tough for the left. South Carolina, a state where voters tend to be more liberal economically but socially moderate, will be the first state to have their primaries in 2028. "It's going to be difficult for a progressive to get out of the primaries and to win the nomination. And a lot of times the money backs the safe candidate. That's, you know, what we saw with Biden in 2020," he said. Still, primaries don’t always come down to the progressive vs. moderate debate, he said, noting that ultimately what matters is any individual candidate and their message. "Somebody like an Obama, it almost doesn't matter where they are politically," he said. Who Else Could Compete for the Progressive Lane? If Ocasio-Cortez opts against running, it’s not clear who would become the progressive front-runner. Many of the leading candidates such as Harris, Newsom, Buttigieg and Ossoff are seen as more moderate Democrats. Sanders has not indicated he would run again, and many progressives have argued it’s time for a younger generation of leaders. At 85, his age could become a concern for progressive voters. Representative Ro Khanna, a California Democrat, is another progressive who has been floated as a presidential candidate but has also trailed in polls. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is ineligible because he does not meet the "natural-born citizen" requirement outlined in Article II of the United States Constitution. Vale said a major lesson from the midterms is that "people don't neatly break down on the ideological lines and litmus tests of folks in DC." "A lot of the candidates who won I would consider more progressive on some issues and more moderate on other issues they don't neatly fit into groups' boxes. And that ability to transcend the policy/political lines will be key to winning," he said. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Robert Greenall and Samantha Beech
news.summary: Strategist Dan Turrentine said there is "almost a consensus" among Democrats El-Sayed will run if AOC passes on 2028.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: ‘Gayest’ Member of Congress Robert Garcia Devotes Quarter of Oversight Staff to Videos, Influencer Outreach

Democrat Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), who once referred to himself as the “gayest” member of Congress, is reportedly using a quarter of committee resources to focus not on affordability but communication, zoning in on influencers, TikTok videos, and more in what has been described as a “presidential-style communication shop.”

Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, is among Democrats who openly admitted that he plans to target Trump officials when Democrats take back power — something Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) and others warned would happen ahead of the midterms. During a recent Crooked Con event in Washington, DC, Garcia essentially attributed this desire, in part, to his so-called “gay… pettiness.”

“Just because you’re Kimberly Guilfoyle, or you’re Kristi Noem, or you’re Pam Bondi, and you’re no longer in office that doesn’t mean that we’re still not interested in accountability for all of your crimes and grift. We’re not going to forget,” he said at the time. “Like, we can’t forget about these folks that are causing harm, like, you know, I think it’s like, maybe it’s because I’m gay, but like, you know, like pettiness is a thing.”

Meanwhile, New York Magazine is detailing Garcia’s role in the future of targeting Trump officials, describing him as “part of the Democratic Party’s version of the Justice League.” He has already met with incoming House Intelligence Committee Chairman Jim Himes (D-CT) and Democrat Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS) — the likely head of the Homeland Security Committee — to discuss dividing up investigations into officials like former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and many, many more personalities.

However, Democrats are struggling to bridge the gap between their visceral desire to investigate Trump officials and their campaign promises to address affordability, the latter of which Americans are primarily focused on as wages fail to keep up with inflation.

Evidently, when Garcia is not thinking about investigations, he is thinking not of affordability but of “how to tell stories” on TikTok with the help of influencers. According to New York Magazine, “A quarter of his committee’s staff is dedicated to communications work: videographers, rapid response, flacks for new media (like influencers), and traditional press.”

“It’s much more like a presidential-style communication shop,” a staff director told the magazine. “No other committee on either side of the Capitol in either party has invested as much time and resources into communications”:

The staff has been thinking about how to package their work for an audience that would never watch a hearing on C-Span but might encounter a clip from one while scrolling through TikTok in bed. “We don’t want to be shouting into the darkness,” Edmonson says.
Garcia tells me he plans on communicating “everywhere,” whether that’s podcasts, Twitch streams, or mainstream media. He’s a regular on cable news and has even appeared on Bravo’s Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen, joking that he’d get to the bottom of some Real Housewives drama with a subpoena. (“Go get ’em,” Andy Cohen messaged him after the midterms.) “He’s been so good at getting attention,” says Rob Flaherty, a Democratic consultant who served as deputy campaign manager for both Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. And Flaherty is of the mind that, as long as the Democrats’ energy is focused, there really is no such thing as going overboard. “I do think more shots on goal is great,” he tells me. “You never know what’s going to break out.”

Garcia came under fire earlier this month after a failed attempt at humor on social media, comparing himself to Pennywise, the fictional, murderous clown character who targets and terrorizes children in Stephen King’s horror novel It, to showcase how “low” he is willing to go against his Republican opponents.
